sections.heading: C — Impaired, distracted and drowsy driving
sections.markdown:
## C — Impaired, distracted and drowsy driving

FACT_ID: sec06-F01 | anchor: A01
The handbook warns that driving experience does not make drinking and driving safe, and that new drivers are more affected by alcohol while still learning. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F02 | anchor: A01
The source treats 12 ounces of beer, five ounces of wine, and a cocktail containing 1.5 ounces of 80-proof spirits as equal alcohol amounts. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F03 | anchor: A01
Drinking and driving can bring heavy fines, higher insurance costs, loss of the license and imprisonment. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F04 | anchor: A01
Blood alcohol concentration describes alcohol in a quantity of blood as a percentage determined by chemical analysis. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F05 | anchor: A01
The amount of alcohol consumed primarily controls how much alcohol reaches the bloodstream; food affects absorption to a lesser extent and drink mixing has only a limited effect. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F06 | anchor: A01
The handbook’s example says two ounces of pure alcohol consumed within an hour produces about the same BAC regardless of the type or mixture of drinks. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F07 | anchor: A01
The handbook’s weight example estimates that a 100-pound person needs about half the alcohol of a 200-pound person to reach the same BAC. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F08 | anchor: A01
People differ in how they react to alcohol, even though the handbook describes general relationships between amount consumed and BAC. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F09 | anchor: A01
The BAC discussion identifies a level of 0.08 or higher, or an illicit or recreational drug’s presence, as conclusive evidence of driving under the influence. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F10 | anchor: A01
A driver can face a DUI charge even with a BAC below 0.08. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F11 | anchor: A01
Refusing chemical testing may result in license revocation. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F12 | anchor: A01
The handbook warns that alcohol possession or consumption before age 21 can cause license revocation even without operating a vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F13 | anchor: A01
The BAC discussion identifies 0.02 BAC as a level requiring revocation for an underage driver. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec06-F14 | anchor: A02
Crash risk rises as BAC increases, and the increase begins before a driver is described as impaired or intoxicated. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F15 | anchor: A02
The handbook says alcohol reaches the brain in 20 to 40 minutes and affects areas controlling judgment and driving skill. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F16 | anchor: A02
Alcohol slows reflexes and reactions, reduces clear vision and alertness, and worsens judgment as the amount in the body increases. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F17 | anchor: A02
Alcohol makes judging distance, speed and other vehicles’ movement more difficult and can interfere with vehicle control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F18 | anchor: A02
The handbook’s advice is to avoid driving after drinking because even one drink can affect driving. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F19 | anchor: A02
A specialty drink may contain as much alcohol as several ordinary drinks. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec06-F20 | anchor: A03
Time is the only way to sober up; coffee, fresh air, exercise and cold showers do not provide a quick remedy. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F21 | anchor: A03
For a social outing, the guide recommends choosing a designated driver who will not drink or using available public transportation or a cab. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F22 | anchor: A03
Food can slow alcohol’s entry into the blood but cannot prevent a person from becoming drunk. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F23 | anchor: A03
Increasing the interval between drinks is identified as the most effective way to slow down alcohol’s effects [A03].
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F24 | anchor: A03
Many prescription and nonprescription drugs can impair driving, sometimes as much as alcohol or more. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F25 | anchor: A03
Medicines taken for headaches, colds, allergies or calming nerves can cause drowsiness that affects driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F26 | anchor: A03
Stimulants and diet pills may briefly increase alertness but can later cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration or vision problems. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F27 | anchor: A03
Before taking a medicine and driving, check its warning label and ask a doctor or pharmacist when unsure about driving-related side effects. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F28 | anchor: A03
The handbook says not to combine alcohol with other drugs because the combination can intensify effects, impair safe driving and cause serious health problems. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F29 | anchor: A03
The handbook reports that marijuana users make more driving mistakes and have more difficulty adapting to glare than other drivers. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec06-F30 | anchor: A04
Doing another task while driving adds to the driver’s mental workload. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F31 | anchor: A04
The source illustrates distraction by saying a vehicle traveling 55 mph covers about a football field while the driver looks away for three to four seconds. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F32 | anchor: A04
Eating, drinking, smoking, changing entertainment, grooming, intense conversations and reading can add more driving tasks than a person can manage safely. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F33 | anchor: A04
Attention to children or pets, retrieving loose objects, calls, texting, electronic messages and selfies can overload attention while driving. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F34 | anchor: A04
Before using an unfamiliar vehicle, adjust the seat and mirrors, choose entertainment settings, and locate the lights, signals and wipers. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F35 | anchor: A04
Long-distance driving can cause drowsiness or reduced awareness, and fatigue slows reactions and dulls thinking. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F36 | anchor: A04
Highway hypnosis describes reduced awareness of surroundings associated with the monotony of driving sounds. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F37 | anchor: A04
When tired while driving, the guide recommends resting or changing drivers. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F38 | anchor: A04
Drowsiness warnings include involuntary eye closure or poor focus, trouble holding the head up, repeated yawning, disconnected thoughts, memory gaps, missed exits, lane drift and variable speed. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-F39 | anchor: A05
Consuming alcohol while driving a motor vehicle on Delaware highways is unlawful. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F40 | anchor: A05
Delaware’s DUI rule reaches a person under alcohol or drug influence who drives, operates or exercises actual physical control over a vehicle, moped or off-highway vehicle anywhere in the state, including highways. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F41 | anchor: A05
Legal entitlement to use alcohol or a drug does not provide a defense to a DUI charge. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F42 | anchor: A05
Driving under alcohol or drug influence can bring both criminal and administrative penalties. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F43 | anchor: A05
A DUI conviction in another state results in revocation of the driver’s Delaware license. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F44 | anchor: A05
The implied-consent passage treats a person arrested for impaired driving, operation or actual physical control of a vehicle, off-highway vehicle or moped as consenting to breath, blood or urine testing. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F45 | anchor: A05
After refusal of the officer-designated test, the source says reasonable steps may be taken to conduct testing without the person’s consent. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F46 | anchor: A05
Chemical-test refusal can lead to a DMV revocation from one to two years, depending on previous DUI, probable-cause or refusal offenses. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F47 | anchor: A05
The juvenile-DUI passage requires Family Court to send the DMV a revocation order lasting until the juvenile reaches age 21. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F48 | anchor: A05
For a person younger than 21 who drives, operates or has actual physical control after consuming alcohol, the zero-tolerance passage assigns a two-month first-offense revocation. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F49 | anchor: A05
A later underage zero-tolerance offense carries revocation for at least six and no more than 12 months. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F50 | anchor: A05
Outside the underage possession-and-consumption subsection’s exceptions, its first-offense fine is $100. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F51 | anchor: A05
Outside that underage possession-and-consumption subsection’s exceptions, each later offense carries a fine from $200 to $500. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-F52 | anchor: A05
The first two violations of the underage possession-and-consumption subsection are civil offenses, and information about them may be absent from a certified criminal record. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0054]

Misconceptions: Preserve the source’s conditions, exceptions and may-versus-must distinction when recalling a rule.
Mnemonics: Use “cause, condition, consequence” as an authored cue for reviewing each cited rule.
Glossary: The key source terms are retained in the individual facts and their domain labels.
Dynamic facts: Contact details, provider lists and current service availability require fresh confirmation and stay outside the stable fact set.

items.skill: Distinguish impairment risks from a legal BAC threshold
items.why: The source permits a DUI charge below the conclusive BAC level and warns against drinking and driving.

items.skill: Apply administrative, court and IID conditions separately
items.why: The handbook gives distinct processes and conditional eligibility tables.

corpus_stability.reason: Working assessment from a single dated official handbook snapshot; actual revision frequency remains unverified debt in part A.
